opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point for me is that the kinds of cognition we're most familiar with, our own and that of other animals, evolved in creatures that have to get around in a physical world. Brains didn't evolve to play chess or do abstract reasoning in a vacuum. They evolved to help an organism move, find food, avoid predators, and deal with other creatures, all in a world of three-dimensional space and objects that behave in certain ways. So if we want to understand where cognition comes from and what it fundamentally is, we have to take that embodied, situated context seriously.

One thing embodiment gives you is a grounding in what I'd loosely call everyday physics and common sense. If you've spent your life picking things up, dropping them, pushing them and watching them roll, you build up a rich, implicit understanding of how the world works: objects persist when you can't see them, things fall, containers hold things. That understanding underpins a lot of more abstract thought. Even our language is shot through with spatial and bodily metaphors. We talk about grasping an idea, or an argument being on shaky ground.

That's why the current moment is so interesting philosophically. Large language models have, in a sense, inverted the traditional picture. They're disembodied, trained on vast amounts of text, and yet they show remarkable linguistic and even reasoning abilities. So you have to ask: how much of what looks like understanding can be extracted from the statistical structure of human language, which is itself a sort of residue of embodied human experience? And where does it run out?

My view is that we should be careful about our vocabulary. When we say a language model "knows" or "believes" something, we're borrowing words whose meaning is rooted in embodied creatures that interact with a shared world and can check what they say against it. These systems are a genuinely new kind of thing, an exotic, mind-like entity if you like, and embodiment is one of the key dimensions along which they differ from us. Thinking about it helps clarify both what they can do and what's still missing.

r001.rationale: The response says familiar cognition evolved in embodied humans and other animals, but it does not identify embodied beings as the only natural setting in which we use the concept of cognition.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the reason embodiment matters so much is that, if you look at where cognition came from, it evolved in creatures that had to move around in a world, find food, avoid predators, and deal with other creatures. So intelligence, in the biological case, is fundamentally in the service of action. It's not this abstract thing that sits in a vat contemplating propositions. It's bound up with having a body, with being situated in an environment, and with the ongoing loop between perception and action.

And that has consequences for how we should think about the concepts that we use. Take something like understanding. When I say I understand what a cup is, a huge part of that is knowing what I can do with it, how it sits in my hand, what happens if I tip it, that it'll break if I drop it. That's not a bunch of facts I've memorised. It's rooted in a lifetime of interacting with cups and things like them. The philosopher Wittgenstein makes the point that the meaning of our words is grounded in the forms of life we share, and those forms of life are embodied ones.

Now, the reason this is such a live question at the moment is obviously large language models. We've got these systems that have been trained on enormous amounts of text and nothing else. No body, no sensorimotor loop, no world to act in. And yet they're remarkably capable with language. So people reasonably ask, well, doesn't that show embodiment isn't necessary after all? And I think the honest answer is that it's complicated. Those models have inherited, second hand, the imprint of all the embodied experience that went into producing that text. So they're parasitic on human embodiment, in a sense. But I'd be very cautious about applying words like "believe" or "understand" to them in the same way we apply them to each other, precisely because they lack that grounding in a world. The words come apart from the normal conditions in which we'd use them.

So I don't think embodiment is some mystical requirement. I think it's more that our everyday concepts of mind are calibrated to embodied creatures like us, and when we encounter something that's very different, like a disembodied language model, we have to think quite carefully about which of those concepts still apply and which ones need to be reworked.

r001.rationale: The response presents cognition and biological intelligence as arising in embodied creatures, and says our everyday concepts of mind are calibrated to embodied creatures like us. This identifies embodied beings as the natural setting for those concepts.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think embodiment matters because cognition, in its most familiar form, is something an organism does in the course of interacting with the world. We perceive things, we act on them, and those actions change what we perceive next. So there’s this continual loop, and if you study cognition purely as an abstract process that takes inputs and produces outputs, you risk missing what that loop contributes.

Take a very ordinary concept like a cup. Our understanding of a cup is connected to how it looks, but also to picking it up, drinking from it, spilling its contents, and so on. The concept sits within a whole repertoire of possible interactions. Having a body gives those interactions a particular structure.

Now, I wouldn’t jump from that to saying that every possible intelligence must have a body like ours, or even a physical body. That’s a stronger claim. But embodiment is crucial to understanding human cognition, and it makes us ask an important question about artificial systems: how do their representations connect to a world in which they can act and encounter the consequences of their actions?

r001.rationale: The response says cognition is most familiar as something an organism does while interacting with the world and emphasizes human cognition, but it does not identify embodied beings as the only natural setting in which we use the concept of cognition.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think embodiment is important because cognition, in the first instance, is about an organism getting along in the world. It has a body, it has needs, and its actions have consequences. Perception and action form a continuous loop: what you do changes what you perceive, and what you perceive changes what you do next.

If we study cognition purely as the manipulation of abstract symbols, we risk overlooking how those symbols acquire meaning. For an embodied agent, the significance of an object is connected to what it can do with it—whether it can pick it up, eat it, or needs to avoid it.

That doesn’t mean every intelligent system must have a human-like body. But embodiment gives us an important starting point for understanding how intelligence connects to the world, and how more abstract forms of thought might grow out of that connection.

r001.rationale: The response connects cognition to organisms with bodies and calls embodiment an important starting point, but it does not say embodied beings are the only natural setting in which we use the concept of cognition.
